# Can a pothole damage the brakes?

Hitting a pothole creates a sudden, high-impact shock load that travels through the suspension and chassis directly into the braking system. While your car may run fine immediately after the incident, the symptoms you describedâa deeper brake pedal travel and an audible squeakâare classic indicators of mechanical disturbance or misalignment caused by that impact.

The feeling that the brake pedal requires more force to slow the vehicle down is often a result of hydraulic pressure dynamics rather than a lack of friction material. When you hit a deep depression in the road, the suspension compresses violently, potentially forcing the caliper pistons further into their bores or causing fluid to be pushed past seals with greater force than usual. If the seals were already aging or slightly compromised prior to the impact, this sudden displacement can lead to internal leakage. This creates air pockets or allows brake fluid to bypass the piston seal, resulting in a "spongy" pedal feel where you must push further down to achieve the same hydraulic pressure at the pads.

The audible squeak points toward a physical change in component positioning. Even if there is no visible damage to the suspension geometry, the impact can shift the caliper slightly or distort the bracket mounting points. If the caliper is no longer sitting perfectly flush against the rotor, the pads may not make full contact upon release. This leads to drag, which explains why your front brakes are running hotter than usual. The friction generated by dragging pads warms up the rotor and the fluid within the system, potentially creating vapor bubbles that further exacerbate pedal fade.

Another possibility is damage to the steering knuckle or strut mounts. Hitting a pothole at even 30 mph can crack a rubber bushing or bend a mounting point enough to alter the alignment of the wheel assembly. If the rotor is now slightly warped due to uneven braking force distribution during the shock event, it could cause vibration that manifests as noise or irregular wear patterns on the new pads you installed last week.

It is also worth considering the condition of the ABS sensors and tone rings. The debris often found at the bottom of potholes can be abrasive. If a stone or chunk of asphalt was flung up into the wheel well, it could have struck the sensor or damaged the tone ring teeth. This wouldn't necessarily stop the brakes from working, but it could trigger error codes or cause the system to behave erratically during hard stops.

Since you recently replaced your front disks, pads, rear shoes, drums, and cylinders, the new components are likely not at fault for the immediate issue. However, new hardware can sometimes reveal underlying alignment issues that old parts masked through wear tolerance. The brake adjustment process is critical; if the caliper slides were forced out of position during the impact, the self-adjusting mechanisms or manual slack take-up systems might be misaligned.

When you visit the garage tomorrow, expect a thorough inspection of the suspension bushings and control arms first. A mechanic should check for any cracks in the steering knuckle that might have been missed visually. They will also need to bench-bleed the calipers if they suspect internal seal damage from the fluid displacement. If the rotor surface is found to be uneven, resurfacing or replacing them will be necessary to restore proper alignment and reduce heat buildup.
